title: Typography and Text Styling
subtitle: Make Your Interfaces Clear, Professional and Easy to Read
description: Learn how CSS controls fonts, text size, weight, spacing, alignment, line height and text decoration. Build a professional application interface while learning how typography affects usability and visual hierarchy.

blocks.text: Welcome to Typography
Open your editor and create a file called index.html.
Today we are going to control how the words inside your interface look and behave.
This topic is called typography.
Typography is not simply about making text beautiful.
Good typography helps a user understand what is important, what can be clicked, and what information belongs together.
Look at the following small application interface.

blocks.title: Our Starting Interface
blocks.code:
Code Academy

Learn programming by building real projects.
blocks.output:
Code Academy
Learn programming by building real projects.
[Start Learning]

blocks.text: Run the page.
The HTML already has meaning and structure, but the text still looks very basic.
CSS will now give that structure a visual hierarchy.
1. Understanding Font Families
The first typography decision is the typeface or font family.
A font family determines the visual shape of letters and numbers.
Use the font-family property to choose one.

blocks.title: Choosing a Font
blocks.output: The page uses Arial when available, with a generic sans-serif fallback.

blocks.text: Notice that we provided more than one value.
If Arial is unavailable, the browser can use another sans-serif font.
This is called a font fallback.
For a real application, choosing a readable font is more important than choosing a complicated font.
A clean interface usually needs consistency more than decoration.
2. Font Size Creates Hierarchy
Now let's control the size of our text.
The property is called font-size.

blocks.title: Creating Different Text Sizes
blocks.output: The heading becomes large, paragraph text stays readable, and the button text remains compact.

blocks.text: Ask yourself why the heading should usually be larger than the paragraph.
The answer is visual hierarchy.
The user should be able to scan the page and quickly understand which text is the title, which text is supporting information, and which text is an action.
This becomes extremely important when you eventually build dashboards, social applications, marketplaces and messaging interfaces.
3. Font Weight Controls Emphasis
Size is not the only way to make text important.
We can also control how thick the characters appear.
The property is font-weight.

blocks.title: Using Font Weight
blocks.output: The course title appears bold while the description uses normal weight.

blocks.text: A value such as 400 commonly represents normal weight.
A value such as 700 commonly represents bold weight.
Do not make everything bold.
If everything is emphasized, nothing feels especially important.
4. Line Height Makes Text Comfortable
Now imagine a paragraph with several lines.
If the lines are packed too closely together, reading becomes uncomfortable.
CSS gives us line-height for controlling the vertical space between lines.

blocks.title: Improving Paragraph Readability
blocks.output: The paragraph gets comfortable vertical spacing between its lines.

blocks.text: A line-height value such as 1.6 is relative to the font size.
This is often easier to maintain than manually choosing a fixed pixel height.
When you build real applications, readability matters because users may spend a long time looking at your interface.
5. Text Alignment
The text-align property controls horizontal alignment.

blocks.title: Aligning Text
blocks.output: Hero text is centered while normal course content remains left aligned.

blocks.text: Common values include left, center, right and justify.
Use alignment because it supports the structure of the interface, not simply because it looks different.
For example, a centered landing-page hero can work well, while a long article is often easier to read when its text is aligned consistently.
6. Text Decoration
Links often appear underlined by default.
CSS lets us control that decoration.

blocks.title: Styling a Link
blocks.output: The browser removes the default underline from the link.

blocks.text: Be careful with this property.
If you remove an underline, the link should still look clearly interactive through other visual cues.
7. Letter Spacing and Word Spacing
Sometimes the letters in a heading need slightly more breathing room.

blocks.title: Letter Spacing
blocks.output: The letters in the brand name receive additional horizontal spacing.

blocks.text: The letter-spacing property changes the space between individual characters.
There is also word-spacing for the space between words.

blocks.title: Word Spacing
blocks.output: The spaces between words become larger.

blocks.text: Use these properties carefully because excessive spacing can make text harder to read.
8. Text Transform
Sometimes the HTML contains normal text, but the design requires uppercase or lowercase presentation.

blocks.title: Changing Text Presentation
blocks.output: The label displays in uppercase while the username keeps its normal text presentation.

blocks.text: The important idea is that CSS can change presentation without changing the original HTML text.
9. Color Is Part of Typography
Typography is also affected by color.
A heading, supporting paragraph and secondary label should not always have exactly the same visual strength.

blocks.title: Creating Text Hierarchy
blocks.output: Primary text is strongest, descriptions are softer, and metadata is visually quieter.

blocks.text: This is how you begin creating a visual hierarchy.
The user should quickly understand what deserves attention first.

11. Combining Typography With the Box Model
Remember the Box Model from the previous lesson.
Typography controls the text itself, while the Box Model controls the space around the element.

blocks.title: Typography Plus Spacing
blocks.output: The heading and paragraph have controlled typography and predictable spacing.

blocks.text: Notice how font-size, line-height and margin work together.
This is how real interfaces are built.
Individual CSS properties are useful, but their real power appears when you combine them to solve a design problem.
12. Build an Application Profile
Let's apply typography to another real interface component.

blocks.title: Profile Structure
blocks.code:
Prince

Frontend Developer

Building modern web applications and learning advanced development.

View Projects
blocks.output: A profile section containing a name, role, biography and action link.

blocks.title: Profile Typography
blocks.output: The profile has a strong name, identifiable role, readable biography and clear project action.

blocks.text: Look at the relationship between the four pieces of text.
The name is the most important identity information.
The role is secondary but still noticeable.
The biography provides detail without competing with the name.
The link tells the user what they can do next.
13. Responsive Typography
Your interface will eventually run on phones, tablets and larger screens.
A heading that looks good on a large screen may become too large on a small phone.

blocks.title: Responsive Heading
blocks.output: The heading uses 36px on larger screens and becomes 28px on screens 600px wide or smaller.

blocks.text: This is one reason responsive design is not only about changing layouts.
Typography must also adapt to the available screen space.
A professional application should remain readable instead of forcing oversized text into a small screen.
14. Typography Debugging Challenge
Imagine that you built a course dashboard.
The headings look weak, the descriptions are difficult to read, and the buttons do not stand out.
Do not randomly change properties.
First identify the problem.
If the heading is too small, think about font-size.
If the heading is not visually strong enough, think about font-weight.
If a paragraph is difficult to read because the lines are crowded, think about line-height.
If the entire interface feels visually flat, think about hierarchy through size, weight and color.

blocks.title: Professional Dashboard Typography
blocks.output: A structured typography system for a learning dashboard.

blocks.text: Run the interface.
Now deliberately change the values and observe what happens.
Make the heading smaller.
Make the description heavier.
Reduce the paragraph line-height.
Then restore the values.
This experiment is important because CSS is learned by observing how rules change the interface.

blocks.question: A course description contains several lines and the lines feel too crowded. Which CSS property should you adjust first?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. line-height controls the vertical spacing between lines of text.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the space from one line of text to the next.
blocks.reasoning: When multiple lines are vertically crowded, line-height is the direct property for improving that spacing.
blocks.hint: Look at the vertical distance between lines.

blocks.question: A dashboard title needs to become more visually important without making it much larger. Which change is the closest solution?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A heavier font-weight can increase emphasis without greatly changing the size.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about making the characters visually stronger.
blocks.reasoning: font-weight controls how heavy or bold the text appears.
blocks.hint: The problem is emphasis, not size.

blocks.question: You are building a mobile dashboard and a large heading takes too much space. Which approach is most appropriate?
options: Use a media query to reduce font-size on smaller screens
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Responsive typography can reduce heading size when the screen becomes smaller.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about adapting the heading to the available screen width.
blocks.reasoning: Media queries allow typography to respond to different screen sizes.
blocks.hint: The problem happens specifically on smaller screens.

blocks.question: A profile page has a person's name, job role and biography. Which hierarchy is most sensible?
options: Biography largest, role medium, name smallest
Name largest, role secondary, biography comfortable and readable
All three should use the same size and weight
Role largest, biography bold, name smallest
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The person's name is the primary identity, while role and biography provide supporting information.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about which piece of information should receive attention first.
blocks.reasoning: Typography should communicate information priority, creating a visual hierarchy.
blocks.hint: Ask yourself what a user should notice first.

blocks.question: You remove the underline from a navigation link. What should you consider next?
options: Make the link impossible to recognize
Provide another clear visual indication that it is interactive
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Interactive elements should remain recognizable even when default decoration is removed.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about how the user will know that the text can be clicked.
blocks.reasoning: Removing decoration is a visual choice, but usability still requires interactive elements to be identifiable.
blocks.hint: Think from the user's point of view.

blocks.question: A small label such as 'COURSE' should appear compact, bold and uppercase. Which combination best matches that goal?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Small size, strong weight and uppercase presentation fit a compact label.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Look for the option that directly controls size, emphasis and capitalization.
blocks.reasoning: The three requirements map directly to font-size, font-weight and text-transform.
blocks.hint: Match each design requirement to its CSS property.

blocks.question: A paragraph is readable in width but its lines are too close together. Which change is most appropriate?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Increasing line-height gives the lines more vertical breathing room.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The issue is the vertical distance between lines.
blocks.reasoning: line-height is specifically designed to control line spacing.
blocks.hint: Do not change the weight when the problem is vertical spacing.

blocks.question: You want the letters in a short brand name to have slightly more space between them. Which property should you use?
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. letter-spacing controls the space between individual characters.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Think about the difference between letters and whole words.
blocks.reasoning: letter-spacing changes character-to-character spacing, while word-spacing changes spaces between words.
blocks.hint: The question says letters, not words.

blocks.question: A developer makes every piece of dashboard text bold because they want the interface to feel important. What is the better approach?
options: Use different sizes, weights and colors to create hierarchy
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Hierarchy works because different elements have different levels of visual importance.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: If everything is emphasized, what happens to the elements that should receive the most attention?
blocks.reasoning: A good typography system creates levels of importance instead of applying the strongest style to everything.
blocks.hint: Think about primary, secondary and supporting information.

blocks.question: A long description in a learning app is difficult to read because each line is packed too tightly. Which solution best addresses the actual problem?
options: Increase line-height while keeping a readable font size
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Line-height improves vertical readability while the font size remains appropriate.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: The issue is not emphasis or capitalization. It is the spacing between lines.
blocks.reasoning: Readable paragraphs need comfortable vertical rhythm, which is controlled primarily by line-height.

blocks.question: You are designing a course card. The title is hard to notice, the description is readable, and the button is clear. Which change should you make first?
options: Increase the title's visual hierarchy using font-size or font-weight
Make the description bold and larger than the title
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. The title should establish the main identity of the card.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Which element should normally communicate the main subject of the card?
blocks.reasoning: Typography should guide the user's eye from primary information to supporting information and finally to actions.
blocks.hint: Start with the element that identifies the content.

blocks.question: You want a page title centered but the normal course content below it should remain left aligned. Which CSS approach is most precise?
options: Set text-align: center on the entire body
Set text-align: center only on the title container
Set font-weight: center on the title
Use letter-spacing to center the content
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Apply alignment to the specific element or container that needs it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Avoid changing alignment for unrelated content.
blocks.reasoning: Targeting the correct element prevents one design decision from accidentally affecting the rest of the page.
blocks.hint: CSS should change the smallest appropriate target.

blocks.text: Final Challenge: Think Like an Interface Developer
You now know much more than how to make text bigger or smaller.
You can use typography to communicate information hierarchy.
You can make paragraphs easier to read.
You can make labels compact and recognizable.
You can make buttons and links easier to understand.
Most importantly, you can make different pieces of information visually communicate their importance.
This is exactly the kind of thinking you will need when we begin combining CSS with JavaScript to create real interactive applications.
HTML gives your application structure.
CSS gives that structure a visual language.
JavaScript will later give the interface behavior.
Your goal is not to memorize CSS properties.
Your goal is to look at a real interface, identify the visual problem, choose the correct CSS concept, and build the solution.
Lesson 5 Complete
You have learned font-family, font-size, font-weight, line-height, text-align, text-decoration, letter-spacing, word-spacing, text-transform and typography hierarchy.
You also applied those concepts to course cards, profiles, dashboards and responsive interfaces.
Next, we will move from typography into one of the most important layout systems in modern CSS: Flexbox.
